text.name: SMB 1 client
text.titlePass: This PC does not connect with the outdated SMB 1
text.titleFail: This PC can connect with the outdated SMB 1
text.why: SMB 1 is a file-sharing protocol from the 1980s with no protection against tampering. A rogue server can talk this PC down to it.
fix: Open Start, type Windows features and open Turn Windows features on or off.
Clear SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support, select OK and restart.
If an old device still needs SMB 1, tell IT: the device should be replaced or updated.

text.name: LLMNR name lookup
text.why: LLMNR asks every device nearby for a name's address and believes the first answer. An attacker on the network uses that to capture sign-ins.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open gpedit.msc > Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client.
Enable "Turn off multicast name resolution".

text.name: NetBIOS name lookup
text.titlePass: NetBIOS names are not looked up by broadcast
text.titleFail: NetBIOS names are looked up by broadcast
text.why: A broadcast name lookup is answered by whoever replies first. An attacker on the network uses that to capture sign-ins.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
It is the value NodeType shown in the details; 2 means names are asked of a name server only.

text.name: Anonymous listing of accounts
text.titlePass: Strangers cannot list the accounts on this PC
text.titleFail: Strangers can list the accounts on this PC
text.why: A list of account names is the first thing needed to guess passwords. Nobody should get it without signing in.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Local Policies > Security Options and enable the first anonymous enumeration setting.

text.name: Anonymous listing of shares
text.titlePass: Strangers cannot list accounts and shared folders
text.titleFail: Strangers can list accounts and shared folders
text.why: Listing shared folders without signing in shows an attacker where to look next.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Local Policies > Security Options and enable the second anonymous enumeration setting.

registry.item: Anonymous listing of accounts and shares blocked

text.name: Anonymous users and Everyone
text.titlePass: Anonymous users do not count as "Everyone"
text.why: Many folders are open to Everyone. With this setting on, that includes people who have not signed in at all.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Local Policies > Security Options and disable the Everyone permissions setting under Network access.

text.name: IP source routing (IPv4)
text.titleFail: Source-routed IPv4 packets are not dropped
text.why: Source routing lets the sender choose a packet's path, which attackers use to get around network defences.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
It is the value DisableIPSourceRouting shown in the details; 2 drops every source-routed packet.

text.name: IP source routing (IPv6)
text.titleFail: Source-routed IPv6 packets are not dropped
text.why: Source routing lets the sender choose a packet's path, which attackers use to get around network defences.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
It is the value DisableIPSourceRouting shown in the details; 2 drops every source-routed packet.

text.name: Anonymous access to pipes and shares
text.titlePass: Shared folders and pipes need a sign-in
text.titleFail: Shared folders and pipes are open without signing in
text.why: Without this, anything listed as open to anonymous users can be reached from the network by anyone, without a password.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Local Policies > Security Options.
Enable "Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares".

registry.item: Anonymous access to pipes and shares restricted

text.name: Plain-text passwords to file servers
text.titlePass: Passwords are never sent to file servers as plain text
text.titleFail: Passwords may be sent to file servers as plain text
text.why: Some old file servers ask for the password unencrypted. Anyone on the network path can then read it.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open secpol.msc > Local Policies > Security Options.
Disable "Microsoft network client: Send unencrypted password to third-party SMB servers".

text.name: NetBIOS name lookups
text.titlePass: Windows never looks up names over NetBIOS
text.titleFail: Windows may look up names over NetBIOS
text.why: Any PC on the network can answer a NetBIOS lookup, pose as the server you meant and collect your sign-in. DNS does the job safely.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open gpedit.msc > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client.
Set "Configure NetBIOS settings" to Enabled, with Disable NetBIOS name resolution.
A device found only by its short name may then need a DNS entry.

absent.found: Not configured (Windows default: off on public networks only)

text.name: Anonymous calls to system services
text.titlePass: Network calls to system services need a sign-in
text.titleFail: System services accept network calls without a sign-in
text.why: Many Windows services answer remote procedure calls. Refusing callers who have not signed in removes a common way to probe and attack them.
fix: This is normally set for all PCs at once: tell IT.
On a single PC, open gpedit.msc > Administrative Templates > System > Remote Procedure Call.
Set "Restrict Unauthenticated RPC clients" to Enabled, with Authenticated.
